title: Motion for Leave to Participate in Oral Argument

pages.text:
No. 25-965
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
Daniel Grand
Petitioner,
v.
City of University Heights, Ohio, et al.
Respondents.
ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT
MOTION OF THE AMERICAN PLANNING ASSOCIATION FOR LEAVE TO
PARTICIPATE IN ORAL ARGUMENT AS AMICUS CURIAE
Pursuant to Rules 21, 28.4, and 28.7 of the Rules of this Court, the
undersigned counsel of record, on behalf of the American Planning Association
("APA") respectfully moves for leave to participate in oral argument in this case as
amicus curiae supporting neither party and requests that the APA be allowed five
minutes of argument time.

2
This case involves the ripeness of claims alleging violations of the First
Amendment, the Fourteenth Amendment, and the Religious Land Use and
Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000 (RLUIPA), 42 U.S.C. 2000cc et seq. APA and
its professional institute, the American Planning Institute of Certified Planners
("AICP") represent nearly 39,000 practicing planners, elected officials and citizens
in state and regional chapters across the United States who are crucially involved
in administering land use matters from their beginnings. See, e.g., Rogin v.
Bensalem Tp. 616 F.2d 680, 698 (3rd Cir. 1980), cert denied, 450 U.S. 1029 (1981)
("land use regulation generally affects a broad spectrum of persons and social
interest and . . . local political bodies are better able than federal courts to assess
the benefits and burdens of such legislation.") Accordingly, the APA is uniquely
suited to provide assistance to the Court not otherwise available. The APA has a
significant interest as its members are on the front lines of implementing the
requirements of RLUIPA, 42 U.S.C. 2000cc-2(f). Therefore, the APA has a
significant interest in preserving the proper application of finality requirements
that can aid in avoiding unnecessary judicial review. In short, RLUIPA does not
replace zoning. See 146 Cong. Rec. S7274-0 at *S7776 (RLUIPA does "not provide
religious institutions with immunity from land use regulation....").
The APA has filed an amicus brief in this Court, arguing that this Court
preserve the finality prong of the test for ripeness as elucidated in Williamson Cnty,
Re. Plan. Comm'12 v. Hamilton Bank of Johnson City, 473 U.S. 172 (1985) and
reaffirmed in Pakdel v. City and Cnty. of San Francisco, 574 U.S. 474 (2021). This

3
appeal is a case of "ifs" rife with speculation. Even if this Court determines that the
Respondent's cease and desist order was a prior restraint or that submitting the
application for the special permit was futile, the APA's argument for preserving the
finality prong for a RLUIPA case, except where futile, is of nationwide importance.
From the very beginning of the application process, planners are typically present.
They educate the public and their local planning and zoning commissions, zoning
boards of appeal, and other land use agencies on administering land use
applications, including those that address religious uses and structures and come
under the aegis of RLUIPA. They are the professionals most likely to be available at
the genesis of an application or land use dispute. They are trained to serve in that
role and are best able to avoid the need for courts to speculate on outcomes by
crystallizing the administrative records necessary for meaningful and effective
judicial review. The APA's participation in oral argument in this case will therefore
be of material assistance to the Court.
Respectfully submitted,
BRIAN R. SMITH
Counsel of Record for American Planning
Association
OCTOBER 29, 2026
